source_row.item_data_json: {"options":{"A":"These findings are most consistent with a benign positional circulation change that can be observed until warmth and pulses return without urgent evaluation.","B":"These findings suggest acute limb ischemia, a vascular emergency requiring rapid recognition and urgent evaluation to preserve tissue and limb viability.","C":"These findings are most consistent with an uncomplicated muscle strain because acute musculoskeletal pain commonly causes pallor and loss of distal pulses.","D":"These findings indicate chronic venous insufficiency because venous disease typically causes sudden pulselessness, coolness, and severe ischemic pain."}}
source_row.rationale: The sudden combination of severe pain, pallor, coolness, and absent pulses is characteristic of acute limb ischemia, which the 2024 multisociety guideline describes as a vascular emergency. Option B correctly identifies the condition and urgency. Option A incorrectly treats ischemic signs as a benign positional change. Option C cannot explain pallor and absent pulses as a simple muscle strain. Option D misclassifies an acute arterial emergency as chronic venous disease.
source_row.source_detail: 2024 AHA/ACC Multisociety Guideline for Lower Extremity PAD — Acute Limb Ischemia: acute hypoperfusion presents with findings including pain, pallor, pulselessness and poikilothermia/coolness and is a vascular emergency requiring rapid recognition and emergency evaluation. 2024 multisociety PAD guideline remains current; rechecked 2026-08-15. NCSBN first-check: Client Needs — Physiological Integrity — Physiological Adaptation: acute/complex alterations, medical emergencies and pathophysiologic adaptation. 2026 NCLEX-RN Test Plan; effective 2026-04-01 through 2029-03-31; currentness rechecked 2026-08-15.

source_row.stem: A client develops sudden severe leg pain with pallor, coolness, and absent distal pulses. Which interpretation is most appropriate?
